module.title: Proofs
module.description: Module 3 covers the machinery of formal proof: the eight standard rules of inference plus four quantifier rules, the four cornerstone proof methods (direct, contrapositive, contradiction, trivial/vacuous), biconditional proofs, and advanced strategies including cases, WLOG, constructive vs nonconstructive existence, counterexamples, uniqueness, and forward vs backward reasoning.

lessons.title: Rules of Inference
lessons.welcome: In Modules 1 and 2 you built precise statements. Now it is time to BUILD ARGUMENTS that go from given premises to a justified conclusion. The atoms of mechanical reasoning are RULES OF INFERENCE — small, named patterns that every formal proof relies on.
objectives: Define a valid argument and explain why valid arguments correspond to tautologies.
Apply the eight standard inference rules: MP, MT, HS, DS, Addition, Simplification, Conjunction, Resolution.
Use the four quantifier rules: UI, UG, EI, EG.
Chain inference rules into multi-step formal proofs.
Recognize the two classic fallacies: affirming the consequent and denying the antecedent.

storytelling.speaker: Student
storytelling.text: Why can't I just check arguments with a truth table?

storytelling.speaker: Professor
storytelling.text: You can — for tiny cases. But truth tables grow exponentially: ten variables means 1024 rows. Inference rules let you build a proof in a number of steps that scales with the argument's complexity, not with the number of variables.

flow.title: Valid argument
flow.content: An argument with premises p₁, …, pₙ and conclusion q is **valid** iff the implication `(p₁ ∧ p₂ ∧ … ∧ pₙ) → q` is a tautology. Equivalently: whenever every premise is true, the conclusion is true.

flow.title: Validity ≠ soundness
flow.content: A **valid** argument has a correct shape — the conclusion follows from the premises whether or not the premises are actually true. A **sound** argument is valid AND has all true premises. Validity is about FORM.

flow.title: The eight standard inference rules
rows: Reject the antecedent when consequent fails
flow.notes: Each rule is a tiny tautology. Chain them to build any formal proof.

flow.title: Inference around campus
items: **MP at KAU:** _'If you submit your CPCS 222 assignment, you receive a grade.'_ + _'You submitted it.'_ ⇒ _'You receive a grade.'_
**MT at Absher:** _'If your iqama is expired, you cannot renew your license.'_ + _'You renewed your license.'_ ⇒ _'Your iqama is not expired.'_
**HS in registration rules:** _'If GPA ≥ 2.0, you may register.'_ + _'If you may register, you receive a schedule.'_ ⇒ _'If GPA ≥ 2.0, you receive a schedule.'_
**DS in exam logistics:** _'You took the morning OR afternoon section.'_ + _'You did not take the morning section.'_ ⇒ _'You took the afternoon section.'_

flow.title: Quantifier inference rules
items: **Universal Instantiation (UI):** ∀x P(x) ⊢ P(c) for any specific c in the domain.
**Universal Generalization (UG):** P(c) for an ARBITRARY c ⊢ ∀x P(x).
**Existential Instantiation (EI):** ∃x P(x) ⊢ P(c) for SOME FRESH c not used elsewhere.
**Existential Generalization (EG):** P(c) ⊢ ∃x P(x).

flow.title: Two classic fallacies — NOT inference rules
items: **Affirming the Consequent — INVALID:** from p → q and q, conclude p. _'It rained → the road is wet. The road is wet. Therefore it rained.'_ — but a sprinkler also wets the road.
**Denying the Antecedent — INVALID:** from p → q and ¬p, conclude ¬q. _'It rained → the road is wet. It did not rain. Therefore the road is not wet.'_ — sprinkler again.

flow.trigger: After the fallacies — the most common student confusion.

exchange.speaker: Student
exchange.text: Affirming the consequent looks just like Modus Ponens. How do I tell them apart?

exchange.speaker: Professor
exchange.text: Direction. MP applies when you have the implication AND the antecedent (`p` is given). The fallacy applies when you have the implication AND the CONSEQUENT (`q` is given). Always ask: is the given fact the LEFT side of the arrow (p) or the RIGHT side (q)? Only the left side gives you MP.

flow.title: Anatomy of a formal proof
flow.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  P1[Premise 1] --> S1[Step]
  P2[Premise 2] --> S1
  S1 -->|rule + line numbers| S2[Step]
  P3[Premise 3] --> S2
  S2 --> S3[Step]
  S3 --> C[Conclusion]

flow.title: How to build a proof
items: 1. Number every line.
2. List the premises first (each labelled 'premise').
3. Each new line cites a RULE NAME and the LINE NUMBERS it depends on.
4. Continue until you reach the conclusion.
5. Mark the end with ∎ or QED.

flow.title: Lab 05 sailing race
flow.source_pattern: Inspired by Lab 05 Q1 — chain inference rules.
flow.problem: Given: (1) `(¬r ∨ ¬f) → (s ∧ d)`, (2) `s → t`, (3) `¬t`. Prove: it rained (`r`).
flow.thinking_process: Modus Tollens twice, plus Addition and De Morgan to glue the steps.
step_by_step_solution: 8. r ∧ f                  De Morgan + double negation (7)
flow.common_mistake: Trying to apply MT to premise 1 directly without first establishing ¬(s ∧ d) on line 6.

flow.title: Quantifier proof — Lab 05 Q2
flow.source_pattern: Inspired by Lab 05 Q2 — UI/UG with propositional rules.
flow.problem: Show that ∀x (P(x) → (Q(x) ∧ S(x))) and ∀x (P(x) ∧ R(x)) imply ∀x (R(x) ∧ S(x)).
flow.thinking_process: Take an arbitrary c, instantiate both premises, combine via MP and Simplification, then UG.
step_by_step_solution: 1. P(c) ∧ R(c)              UI on second premise
4. P(c) → Q(c) ∧ S(c)       UI on first premise
flow.common_mistake: Forgetting to mark c as ARBITRARY at the start — UG at line 8 would be invalid otherwise.

flow.title: Identify the rule
flow.source_pattern: Inspired by Lab 04 Q12 / Lab 05 Q4 — name the rule.
flow.problem: Identify the rule used: 'If it snows, the school closes. The school is open. Therefore it did not snow.'
flow.thinking_process: Premises: p → q, ¬q. Conclusion: ¬p. Match the pattern.
step_by_step_solution: Let p = 'it snows', q = 'the school closes'.
flow.common_mistake: Calling this denying the antecedent. The given fact is ¬q (consequent denied), so MT applies.

flow.title: Common student mistakes
items: Affirming the consequent and denying the antecedent — they look like MP/MT but are NOT valid.
Reusing an existing name in EI. The witness must be a NEW constant.
Applying UG to a specifically-named element. UG requires ARBITRARY c.
Skipping rule citations on intermediate lines.

flow.title: Six-rule shortlist
items: **MP:** trigger fires (p is given) ⇒ obligation fires (q).
**MT:** obligation fails (¬q) ⇒ trigger never fired (¬p).
**DS:** one disjunct down ⇒ the other holds.
**HS:** chain two implications.
**Resolution:** cancel a literal across disjunctions.
**UI/EI:** instantiate. **UG/EG:** generalize.

sections.heading: Valid arguments
sections.explanation: An argument is valid iff (premises → conclusion) is a tautology.

sections.heading: Eight propositional rules
sections.explanation: MP, MT, HS, DS, Addition, Simplification, Conjunction, Resolution.

sections.heading: Quantifier rules
sections.explanation: UI/UG instantiate/generalize universals; EI/EG handle existentials with fresh witnesses.

worked_examples.problem: From (p → q), p infer q. Name the rule.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Mixing up MP with affirming the consequent.

quick_checks.question: From p ∨ q and ¬p ∨ r, Resolution yields:
From p → q and q, you can conclude p.

key_takeaways: Validity is about argument shape; soundness adds true premises.
Eight propositional rules: MP, MT, HS, DS, Addition, Simplification, Conjunction, Resolution.
Quantifier rules: UI, UG, EI, EG. EI requires a fresh constant; UG requires arbitrary c.
Affirming the consequent and denying the antecedent are invalid — common exam traps.
A formal proof = numbered, justified sequence ending at the conclusion.

lessons.title: Introduction to Proofs
lessons.welcome: Inference rules are the alphabet; PROOFS are the literature. A proof transforms a CONJECTURE into a THEOREM — and once proved, it stays proved forever. This lesson covers the four cornerstone proof methods: direct, contrapositive, contradiction, and the special-case trivial/vacuous proofs.
objectives: Distinguish theorem, axiom, lemma, corollary, conjecture, and proof.
Produce a direct proof of an implication p → q.
Produce a proof by contradiction by assuming ¬claim.
Recognize trivial and vacuous proofs and prove biconditional statements.

storytelling.speaker: Student
storytelling.text: When is contraposition better than direct proof?

storytelling.speaker: Professor
storytelling.text: When the hypothesis is hard to manipulate but its negation is easy. Try proving 'if n² is odd, then n is odd' directly — you'd have to factor an odd square. Contraposition flips it: 'assume n is even, show n² is even', which is one line of algebra.

flow.title: Vocabulary of mathematical writing
rows: A claim that has been proven true
A foundational truth taken without proof
A 'helper' theorem used inside a larger proof
An immediate consequence of a theorem
A statement believed true but unproven
A finite, justified sequence of statements ending at the claim

flow.title: Definitions you'll use throughout Module 3
items: **n is even** iff there exists an integer k with `n = 2k`.
**n is odd** iff there exists an integer k with `n = 2k + 1`.
**r is rational** iff there exist integers p, q (q ≠ 0) with `r = p/q`. Otherwise r is **irrational**.

flow.title: Direct proof
flow.content: To prove `p → q` directly, **assume p**, then use definitions, axioms, and previously proven theorems to **derive q**. Skeleton: `Assume p. … Therefore q. ∎`.

flow.title: Direct proof — sum of two evens is even
flow.source_pattern: Inspired by Lab 05 Q7 / Assignment 1 Q6 — direct proof template.
flow.problem: Show that the sum of two even integers is even.
flow.thinking_process: Assume both even, write each as 2k, factor out the 2.
step_by_step_solution: Let m and n be even. By definition, m = 2a and n = 2b for some integers a, b.
Since a + b is an integer, m + n has the form 2k, so m + n is even.
flow.common_mistake: Writing m = 2a and n = 2a (same letter) — the two integers may differ; use different multipliers.

flow.title: Proof by contraposition
flow.content: To prove `p → q`, prove the **logically equivalent** `¬q → ¬p`. Skeleton: `Assume ¬q. … Therefore ¬p. By contraposition, p → q. ∎`.

flow.title: Contrapositive — n² odd ⇒ n odd
flow.problem: For any integer n, prove that if n² is odd, then n is odd.
flow.thinking_process: Direct is messy. Contrapositive: assume n is even, show n² is even.
step_by_step_solution: We prove the contrapositive: 'if n is even, then n² is even.'
Assume n is even, so n = 2k for some integer k.
Since 2k² is an integer, n² is even.
By contraposition, n² odd ⇒ n odd. ∎
flow.common_mistake: Forgetting the closing line 'by contraposition' — without it the reader sees only the contrapositive.

flow.title: Proof by contradiction (reductio ad absurdum)
flow.content: To prove a claim `p`, assume `¬p` and derive a CONTRADICTION (something of the form `r ∧ ¬r`). Since ¬p leads to absurdity, ¬p must be false, so p is true. For an implication `p → q`, assume `p ∧ ¬q` and derive any contradiction.

flow.trigger: After contradiction is introduced — the canonical √2 question.

exchange.speaker: Student
exchange.text: Why does the √2 proof always start with 'in lowest terms'?

exchange.speaker: Professor
exchange.text: Because the contradiction lives there. We derive that both `a` and `b` are even, which means the fraction `a/b` was NOT in lowest terms after all. Without the 'lowest terms' assumption, the both-even conclusion is harmless. The contradiction is between 'lowest terms' and 'both even'.

flow.title: Contradiction — √2 is irrational
flow.source_pattern: Classical proof, used in Module 3 lecture (Sec 1.7).
flow.thinking_process: Suppose √2 = a/b in lowest terms. Show a and b are both even — contradicting lowest terms.
step_by_step_solution: Suppose for contradiction that √2 is rational, so √2 = a/b in lowest terms (gcd(a, b) = 1).
Square: 2 = a²/b², so a² = 2b². Hence a² is even, which (by the previous theorem) implies a is even. Write a = 2c.
Substitute: (2c)² = 2b², so 4c² = 2b², so b² = 2c². Hence b² is even, so b is even.
Now both a and b are even, sharing the factor 2 — contradicting gcd(a, b) = 1.
The assumption is impossible, so √2 is irrational. ∎
flow.common_mistake: Forgetting 'in lowest terms' — without it the both-even conclusion is not a contradiction.

flow.title: Trivial vs vacuous proofs
rows: 'If it rains, the empty set is a subset of every set.' (Conclusion is always T.)
'If 1 + 1 = 3, then your grandma wears combat boots.' (Hypothesis is always F.)
flow.notes: Both are valid implications even though they sound silly. Trivial and vacuous proofs are common BASE CASES inside induction (Module 10).

flow.title: Biconditional proofs
flow.content: To prove `p ↔ q`, prove BOTH directions: (⇒) `p → q` and (⇐) `q → p`. Each direction may use a different method (direct, contrapositive, contradiction).

flow.title: Biconditional — n is odd iff n² is odd
flow.problem: Prove: for integer n, n is odd ⇔ n² is odd.
flow.thinking_process: (⇒) direct from 'n odd ⇒ n² odd'. (⇐) reuse the contrapositive proof above.
step_by_step_solution: (⇒) Assume n is odd: n = 2k + 1. Then n² = (2k + 1)² = 4k² + 4k + 1 = 2(2k² + 2k) + 1, which is odd.
(⇐) From the previous worked example: n² odd ⇒ n odd by contraposition.
flow.common_mistake: Proving only one direction. Both are needed.

flow.title: Common student mistakes
items: Assuming the conclusion in a direct proof — q is what you must DERIVE, not start with.
Confusing contrapositive with converse. Only the contrapositive is logically equivalent.
Missing the contradiction in a 'proof by contradiction'. The contradiction must be of form `r ∧ ¬r`.
Proving only one direction of a biconditional.

flow.title: Method shortlist
items: **Direct:** assume p, derive q.
**Contrapositive:** assume ¬q, derive ¬p.
**Contradiction:** assume ¬claim, derive r ∧ ¬r.
**Trivial:** q is always T. **Vacuous:** p is always F.
**Biconditional:** prove both directions.

sections.explanation: Theorem, axiom, lemma, corollary, conjecture, proof.

sections.heading: Direct and contrapositive
sections.explanation: Direct: assume p, derive q. Contrapositive: assume ¬q, derive ¬p — equivalent.

sections.heading: Contradiction, trivial, vacuous, biconditional
sections.explanation: Each method targets a different proof shape.

worked_examples.problem: Show: sum of two odd integers is even.
step_by_step_solution: Since a + b + 1 is an integer, the sum is even.
worked_examples.final_answer: Sum of two odd integers is even. ∎
worked_examples.why_it_works: Pair the +1 terms; the result is divisible by 2.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Using same letter for both: m = 2a + 1, n = 2a + 1 (forces them to be equal).

quick_checks.explanation: Direct would require factoring an odd square.

quick_checks.question: A proof of p ↔ q requires:
Vacuous proof shows q is always true.

key_takeaways: Theorem (proven), axiom (accepted), lemma (helper), corollary (immediate consequence), conjecture (unproven), proof (justified chain).
Contrapositive: prove ¬q → ¬p (logically equivalent to p → q).
Trivial: q always T. Vacuous: p always F.

lessons.title: Proof Methods and Strategy
lessons.welcome: By now you have direct, contrapositive, and contradiction proofs. Real theorems often require more: splitting an argument into CASES, exploiting symmetry with WLOG, demonstrating WITNESSES for existence claims, proving UNIQUENESS, and choosing forward or backward reasoning.
objectives: Construct proofs by cases and verify exhaustiveness.
Use 'without loss of generality' (WLOG) correctly when cases are symmetric.
Distinguish constructive from nonconstructive existence proofs.
Disprove a universal claim with a single counterexample.
Prove uniqueness (∃!x) by combining existence with 'any two are equal'.
Choose between forward and backward reasoning for a given goal.

storytelling.speaker: Student
storytelling.text: What's the difference between constructive and nonconstructive existence proofs?

storytelling.speaker: Professor
storytelling.text: Constructive gives you the witness explicitly. 'There exists a sum of two cubes equal to a number in two different ways' — yes, 1729 = 1³ + 12³ = 9³ + 10³. Nonconstructive proves a witness MUST exist without telling you which. They are equally rigorous; constructive is more informative when available.

flow.title: Proof by cases
flow.content: When the hypothesis splits into a finite, EXHAUSTIVE set of subcases p₁ ∨ p₂ ∨ … ∨ pₙ, prove the conclusion in each case separately. Cases must cover every possibility — missing one invalidates the proof.

flow.title: Cases — n² ≥ n for every integer
flow.problem: Prove: for every integer n, n² ≥ n.
flow.thinking_process: Split by sign: n ≥ 1, n = 0, n ≤ -1.
step_by_step_solution: Case 1: n ≥ 1. Then n² = n · n ≥ n · 1 = n.
flow.common_mistake: Skipping n = 0. Boundary cases are easy to miss.

flow.title: Without loss of generality (WLOG)
flow.content: When two or more cases are STRUCTURALLY IDENTICAL except for relabeling, prove one and assert the other 'without loss of generality'. The phrase signals: 'this argument works for the symmetric case verbatim'. Use only when cases are TRULY symmetric.

flow.title: WLOG — even product/sum
flow.problem: If both x · y and x + y are even, then both x and y are even.
flow.thinking_process: Contrapositive: assume not both even. WLOG x is odd. Then split on y's parity.
step_by_step_solution: WLOG x is odd. Write x = 2m + 1.
Case A: y even, y = 2n. x + y = 2(m + n) + 1 is odd.
Case B: y odd, y = 2n + 1. x · y = (2m + 1)(2n + 1) = 2(2mn + m + n) + 1 is odd.
In either case, one of x · y, x + y is odd.
flow.final_answer: Both x and y must be even. ∎
flow.common_mistake: Using WLOG when cases are not actually symmetric.

flow.title: Existence proofs — constructive vs nonconstructive
items: **Constructive:** explicitly produce a witness c with P(c).
**Nonconstructive:** prove a witness must exist without producing it (often via case analysis or contradiction).

flow.title: Constructive existence — Hardy-Ramanujan
flow.problem: Show there is a positive integer expressible as a sum of two cubes in two different ways.
flow.common_mistake: Listing the witness without verifying both representations equal.

flow.title: Counterexample — every prime is odd
flow.thinking_process: Find one prime that is even.
step_by_step_solution: 2 is prime (its only positive divisors are 1 and 2).
flow.final_answer: 2 is a counterexample. The claim is false. ∎
flow.common_mistake: Pretending more cases are needed. ONE counterexample is enough.

flow.title: Uniqueness proofs
flow.content:
To prove `∃!x P(x)` (there is a unique x with P(x)), do TWO things:
- **Existence:** produce some x with P(x).
- **Uniqueness:** assume P(x) and P(y), then derive x = y.

flow.title: Uniqueness — linear equation
flow.problem: For real a ≠ 0, b, show ax + b = 0 has a unique real solution.
flow.thinking_process: Existence: x = -b/a. Uniqueness: any two solutions are equal.
step_by_step_solution: Existence: x = -b/a satisfies a(-b/a) + b = -b + b = 0.
Uniqueness: suppose s also satisfies as + b = 0. Then a(-b/a) = as. Divide by a ≠ 0: s = -b/a.

flow.title: Strategy ladder — pick a method
rows: Pick arbitrary c, prove P(c), apply UG

flow.trigger: After the strategy ladder — the practical question that always comes up.

exchange.speaker: Student
exchange.text: When should I use forward vs backward reasoning?

exchange.speaker: Professor
exchange.text: Forward when the hypothesis is rich and the path forward is clear: chain consequences. Backward when the conclusion suggests sufficient conditions you know how to prove: keep asking 'what would suffice?' until you reach something you already have. Most real proofs combine both, meeting in the middle.

flow.title: Common student mistakes
items: Cases that are not exhaustive (missing zero or boundary).
Using WLOG when cases are merely similar, not truly symmetric.
Skipping the uniqueness step.
Trying to disprove ∀ by 'mostly fails'. ONE counterexample is required.
Building proofs only forward when backward reasoning would shortcut.

flow.title: Method picker (5 seconds)
items: **∀ goal:** pick arbitrary c, prove P(c), UG.
**¬∀ goal:** hunt for one counterexample.
**∃ goal:** produce a witness (or nonconstructive case-split).
**∃! goal:** existence + uniqueness.
**p ↔ q goal:** both directions.

sections.heading: Cases and WLOG
sections.explanation: Split into exhaustive cases; WLOG only when cases are symmetric.

sections.heading: Existence and uniqueness
sections.explanation: Constructive vs nonconstructive existence; uniqueness needs two halves.

sections.heading: Counterexamples and strategy
sections.explanation: ONE counterexample disproves ∀. Strategy ladder + forward/backward reasoning.

worked_examples.problem: Disprove: every positive integer is the sum of three squares.
step_by_step_solution: 7 cannot be written as a² + b² + c² for non-negative integers a, b, c (max with a, b, c ≤ 2 is 4 + 4 + 4 = 12; check all combinations sum to 0..12 but not 7).
worked_examples.common_mistake: Trying to enumerate all combinations exhaustively in writing — one is enough.

quick_checks.question: Cleanest way to disprove 'every prime is odd':
WLOG can be used whenever two cases look similar.

key_takeaways: WLOG only when cases are structurally symmetric.
Constructive existence: produce a witness. Nonconstructive: prove one must exist.
Strategy: direct → contrapositive → contradiction → cases → constructive ∃ → nonconstructive ∃ → counterexample for ¬∀.
Forward grows from hypothesis; backward grows from conclusion — combine.

Define 'valid argument' formally.
questions.answer: An argument is valid iff (p₁ ∧ … ∧ pₙ) → q is a tautology — every truth assignment making all premises true also makes q true.

questions.question: Why does EI require a fresh constant?
questions.answer: Because the witness from ∃x P(x) is unknown. Reusing an existing name would assert facts about a specific known element, not a new witness.

questions.question: Direct proof: square of any odd integer is odd.
Why is 'direct first' a sensible default?
questions.answer: Direct proofs are usually the most informative; contraposition rephrases the goal but doesn't add power; contradiction often hides why a result is true. Try the cleanest path first.

questions.question: Difference between exhaustive and disjoint cases?
questions.answer: Exhaustive = every possibility falls into at least one case (REQUIRED). Disjoint = cases don't overlap (NOT required, just stylistic).
questions.explanation: Coverage matters; uniqueness of case is optional.

questions.question: MP: from p → q and ___, conclude q.
MT: from p → q and ___, conclude ¬p.
Resolution: from p ∨ q and ¬p ∨ r, conclude ___.
Direct proof of p → q: assume ___, derive q.
Contrapositive of p → q: prove ___ → ___.
Reorder these proof lines to show that from {¬r ∨ ¬f → s ∧ d, s → t, ¬t}, conclude r.
items: ¬s ∨ ¬d  (Addition from ¬s)
(¬r ∨ ¬f) → (s ∧ d)  (premise)
s → t  (premise)
¬t  (premise)
¬s  (MT from s → t and ¬t)
¬(s ∧ d)  (De Morgan)
r ∧ f  (De Morgan + double negation)
r  (Simplification)
questions.explanation: Premises first, then derived steps in dependency order.

questions.question: Use rules to show: from premises 'If you send me an email, I finish the program', 'If you do not send me an email, I go to bed early', and 'If I go to bed early, I wake up refreshed', conclude 'If I do not finish the program, I wake up refreshed'.
questions.answer:
Let e, p, b, w. Premises: e → p, ¬e → b, b → w.
4. ¬p → ¬e   (contrapositive of premise 1)
5. ¬e → w    HS (¬e → b, b → w)
6. ¬p → w    HS (4, 5). ∎
questions.explanation: Two HS applications via the contrapositive of the first premise.

questions.question: Direct proof: product of two rationals is rational.
questions.answer: Let r, s rationals. r = p/q, s = t/u with q, u ≠ 0 integers. r·s = pt/qu. Since pt is an integer and qu ≠ 0 is an integer, r·s is rational. ∎

questions.question: Contrapositive: if x + y ≥ 2 (real x, y), then x ≥ 1 or y ≥ 1.
questions.answer: Contrapositive: if x < 1 AND y < 1, then x + y < 2. Direct: x < 1 and y < 1 ⇒ x + y < 1 + 1 = 2. ∎
questions.explanation: Disjunctive conclusion → conjunctive hypothesis under contraposition.

questions.question: Cases: for every integer n, n² + n is even.
questions.answer:
Case n even, n = 2k: n² + n = 4k² + 2k = 2(2k² + k), even.
Case n odd, n = 2k + 1: n² + n = 4k² + 4k + 1 + 2k + 1 = 4k² + 6k + 2 = 2(2k² + 3k + 1), even.
Cases exhaust ℤ. ∎

questions.question: Identify the rule used: (a) 'If snow, school closes. School open. Therefore no snow.' (b) 'If swim, sunburn. Swam. Therefore sunburned.' (c) 'Rain or sunny. Not raining. Therefore sunny.' (d) 'A → B. B → C. Therefore A → C.'
Show: from ∀x (P(x) ∨ Q(x)), ∀x (¬Q(x) ∨ S(x)), ∀x (R(x) → ¬S(x)), and ∃x ¬P(x), conclude ∃x ¬R(x).
questions.answer:
1. ∃x ¬P(x)   premise
2. ¬P(c)   EI (1), c fresh
3. P(c) ∨ Q(c)   UI on first premise
4. Q(c)   DS (2, 3)
5. ¬Q(c) ∨ S(c)   UI on second premise
6. S(c)   DS (4, 5)
7. R(c) → ¬S(c)   UI on third premise
8. ¬R(c)   MT (6, 7)
9. ∃x ¬R(x)   EG (8). ∎
questions.explanation: EI for fresh witness; UI for universals; DS, MT, EG.

questions.question: Show [p ∧ (p → q)] → q is a tautology using equivalences (no truth table).
Use proof by contradiction to show there is no largest prime.
questions.answer: Suppose largest prime is p. Form r = 2 · 3 · 5 · ⋯ · p + 1. Each pᵢ leaves remainder 1 when dividing r, so no pᵢ divides r. So r is prime or has a prime factor not in our list — contradicting 'p was largest'. ∎

questions.question: Use rule of inference: 'There is an employee in the factory who must attend training' from premises 'Some employee violated a policy' and 'Every employee who violated a policy must attend training'.
questions.answer:
1. ∃x (E(x) ∧ V(x))   premise
2. E(c) ∧ V(c)   EI (1), c fresh
3. E(c)   Simplification (2)
4. V(c)   Simplification (2)
5. ∀x ((E(x) ∧ V(x)) → T(x))   premise (rephrased)
6. (E(c) ∧ V(c)) → T(c)   UI (5)
7. T(c)   MP (2, 6)
8. ∃x (E(x) ∧ T(x))   EG with E(c) ∧ T(c). ∎
questions.explanation: EI for existential; UI for universal; MP; EG.

questions.template: From premises {PREMISE1} and {PREMISE2}, what conclusion follows by {RULE}?
questions.instructions: Pick (PREMISE1, PREMISE2, RULE) where the rule actually applies; identify the conclusion.

CLAIM: If n² is even, then n is even.
There exist irrationals x, y with x^y rational.
For every integer n, n² + n is even.
Every prime greater than 2 is odd.

questions.instructions: Match claim to method (direct, contrapositive, contradiction, cases, constructive ∃, nonconstructive ∃).
questions.example_realization: 'If n² is even, then n is even' → contrapositive.

ARGUMENT: If it rains the road is wet. The road is wet. Therefore it is raining.
If it rains the road is wet. It is raining. Therefore the road is wet.
If it rains the road is wet. The road is not wet. Therefore it is not raining.
Either you study or you fail. You did not study. Therefore you failed.

questions.instructions: MP/MT/DS valid; affirming the consequent and denying the antecedent are fallacies.
questions.example_realization: 'Road is wet → therefore raining' = affirming the consequent — FALLACY.
questions.explanation: Drill on the two main fallacies.
